turns.action: I ask the woman in the saffron work scarf what her name is and whether she knows
turns.narration:
You ask the woman her name and whether she saw who carried the sealed case toward the far lift. Your gear settles against your shoulders as you stand beside the repair bench; the wrench pauses against the coupling, and the bay’s low reactor hum fills the gap.

“Ressa. I saw them take it to the lift.” She gives you a brief, polite glance, then wipes her grease-dark fingers on a rag and returns to the coupling. Beyond the partition, the far lift remains shut, its indicator dark. The dry double knock sounds again from the service corridor.

turns.action: I examine the far lift’s dark indicator and inspect its doors and frame for sign
turns.narration:
You examine the far lift’s dark indicator, then run your gloved fingers along the doors and frame. Dust coats the seams, but a fresh crescent of grease marks the lower edge; two bright scratches cut through the grime beside the manual release. The double knock sounds again from the service corridor, followed by a pause.

You search the corridor around its source. Boot prints cross the dusty grating toward a maintenance hatch, and a small brass fastener lies beside the wall—matching the type fitted to the sealed case’s clasp. As you crouch to inspect it, your sleeve catches the hatch’s jagged lip and tears at the cuff. Ressa keeps her attention on the coupling, wrench turning in short, even pulls.

The prints end at the hatch. A thin line of fresh grease runs beneath its closed edge, and another cautious double knock comes from the other side.

turns.narration:
You brace your boot against the wall and wrench the maintenance hatch open, keeping your weight set to slam it shut. The manual catch gives with a metallic snap. The hatch jerks outward against your hands, wrenching your torn cuff farther up your wrist, and the edge strikes your forearm hard enough to numb your grip. Your boot skids on the grating. You lose the leverage and the hatch drops back into its frame with a bang.

A muffled scrape comes from beyond it, then silence. At the repair bench, Ressa looks from the matching brass fastener in your hand to the torn sleeve. She sets down her wrench. “Before I tell you anything about that passage: keep this hatch shut and the repair bay clear. We can’t spare parts or people for a breach.” Her eyes stay on your face; one grease-blackened thumb presses against the bench edge.

The reactor hum fills the pause. Dust shifts under your boot, and your forearm throbs where the hatch struck it. Ressa picks up the wrench again but does not turn back to the coupling. Between you, the hatch sits closed, its manual catch exposed.

turns.action: I brace my bruised forearm against the hatch frame and wrench the exposed manual
turns.narration:
You brace your bruised forearm against the frame and wrench the exposed catch toward its locking position, putting your weight into it. The catch grinds halfway, then slips from your fingers. The hatch jumps outward against your shoulder with a hard clang; pain flashes through your forearm, and your grip opens. From the corridor side, scraping stops. The lock remains unseated, and the catch’s bent tip no longer fits cleanly into its bracket.

Ressa backs from the hatch, jaw tight. “I need a pry bar and a fresh retaining pin. I’ve got wire, not a pin.” She lifts a short coil from the bench, then holds it out without stepping closer. “The case has a pressure seal. Don’t force it.” The thin wire is the only spare material within reach; the pry bar lies beneath a heap of cargo straps.

The bay’s recycled air tastes of metal as you ease your arm away from the frame. Ressa returns to the bench and clears a space for the wire. Beyond the skewed catch, the corridor stays quiet, and the choice between securing the hatch with what you have and leaving it exposed remains yours.

turns.narration:
You haul the cargo straps off the pry bar and drag it free, then wedge its tip beneath the bent catch and lean into the lever, keeping clear of the sealed case. The catch twists out of its bracket with a sharp crack. The hatch kicks away from the frame and knocks the pry bar from your hands. It lands beyond the docking bay’s waist-high cargo partition, out of reach; you and Ressa are left on opposite sides as the hatch hangs crooked and unsecured.

A heavy step sounds in the corridor, followed by a demand through the metal: “Open up.” Ressa takes the wire from the bench but stays where she is, watching your hands. “That case stays sealed. I’ll hold the wire ready, but I won’t help you force anything.” She turns toward the narrow gap between stacked crates, leaving the repair bay and the pry bar behind.

The pressure seal remains untouched. Your forearm throbs, the bay presses close with cargo and recycled air, and the demand comes again from beyond the hatch. The wire lies within reach on Ressa’s abandoned side of the partition.

turns.narration:
You shove the stack of crates hard against the crooked hatch. They scrape over the grating and jam beneath its lower edge as the figure outside drives the hatch inward. The crates hold; the figure’s shoulder and sealed case remain visible through the narrow gap. Your leg takes the strain, then buckles under the blow. Pain flares where you were struck, and you stagger back, favoring one leg as the hatch settles against the crates.

The figure stops forcing the gap. “I’m carrying this case through,” it says, keeping one hand on the hatch. Before you can answer, a dry double knock sounds from the service corridor behind you. Ressa looks toward it, then at your uneven stance. She stays beside the bench, her hands clear of the wire. The docking bay’s strip lights buzz over the displaced cargo, and no one moves to clear a path.

The crates hold for now, the crooked hatch pinned against them, while the figure waits at the gap and the service-corridor knock goes unanswered.

turns.action: ## I was being cautious, not aggressive
turns.narration:
You ease a crate across the grating and wedge it beneath the crooked hatch, keeping your bruised forearm clear of the catch. The figure pushes from the corridor side. The crate shudders under the pressure, then holds the hatch a handspan from the frame. A slat splits with a dry crack; the gap stays open, but the hatch no longer swings wider.

“Please let me through with the case,” the figure says, its tone level. Ressa keeps her distance from the sealed case and looks from your braced crate to the figure. “I won’t force it,” she says. “I can hold the hatch while you speak.” She sets the wire down and places both hands against the frame, careful not to touch the case.

The figure withdraws its shoulder. The hatch rests against the crate while Ressa steadies the frame, and for a few breaths the docking bay holds only reactor hum, recycled-air hiss, and the cramped quiet between you. The visitor waits at the gap for your answer.
